summary: Scott Stephenson, CEO of Deepgram, opens with a company overview: Deepgram has been building audio AI for nine years, bringing end-to-end deep learning to speech recognition, and recently launched a TTS product in December. Their API supports on-prem and cloud deployment with model adaptation to specific acoustic environments (e.g., drive-thrus with background noise). Deepgram is research-led and powers devices and services including Spotify, food ordering, and call centers, claiming to be the largest Speech-to-Text API in the world. Stephenson frames the field's evolution from Voice AI 1.0 (slow, inaccurate, domain-specific systems like Siri) to Voice AI 2.0 (open-ended, LLM-powered conversational agents). The current architecture is a pipeline: speech-to-text, then text-to-text (LLM), then text-to-speech—which he internally calls 'text the text.' He compares the current moment to seeing the first cars in 1910, predicting a 100x explosion in voice AI over the next decade. He frames this within a revolution timeline: Agricultural (1000-2000 years), Industrial (250-300 years), Information (75 years), and Intelligence (25-30 years), arguing AI companies must move three times faster than traditional tech companies. Current state-of-the-art figures include speech recognition accuracy improving from ~75% five-to-eight years ago to over 90% today, and latency dropping from 2-5 seconds to 100-200 milliseconds. A blog post from Daily demonstrated a full voice AI roundtrip under 500ms using Deepgram, Llama, and Deepgram TTS—comparable to human turn-taking at 400-600ms. The critical gap Stephenson identifies is context: current pipeline components do not pass context to each other, causing 10-20% of turns to misfire. He proposes 'contextual AI,' where each stage accepts and outputs context (text, audio, images, embeddings), enabling the system to sense emotion, conversation pace, background sounds, and speaker intent. This contextual flow will make agents feel genuinely human. He notes that while unified speech-to-speech models exist, they sacrifice controllability, which businesses like banks require. He advocates for compartmentalized architectures and COGS optimization through right-sizing each component. Stephenson closes by announcing Deepgram's full-stack voice AI agent product, available in preview. Customers can use their own API keys and LLMs or use Deepgram end-to-end, with the integrated approach reducing turn-taking latency to 300-600ms versus 800-1500ms when self-pieced. Deepgram offers $250 in trial credits, and a workshop was given by Damen two days prior.

sections.title: Introduction to Deepgram
sections.summary: Stephenson introduces Deepgram as a 9-year-old audio AI company that brought end-to-end deep learning to speech recognition, recently launched a TTS product, supports on-prem and cloud deployment with acoustic environment adaptation, and is research-led. He notes Deepgram powers many devices and services behind the scenes and sets the bar at 'what can a human do.'

sections.title: Voice AI Evolution: From 1.0 to 2.0
sections.summary: Stephenson contrasts Voice AI 1.0 (slow, inaccurate, domain-specific, like Siri) with Voice AI 2.0 (open-ended, LLM-powered). He describes the current pipeline as speech-to-text to text-to-text (LLM) to text-to-speech, which he internally calls 'text the text.' He compares the current moment to 1910 when first cars appeared, predicting a 100x explosion in voice AI over the next decade.

sections.title: Revolution Timeline and Current State of the Art
sections.summary: Stephenson frames revolutions by duration: Agricultural (1000-2000 years), Industrial (250-300 years), Information (75 years), Intelligence (25-30 years), arguing AI companies must move 3x faster than tech companies. Current SOTA: speech recognition over 90% accuracy (up from ~75%), latency down to 100-200ms (from 2-5s), and full roundtrip under 500ms demonstrated by Daily, matching human turn-taking at 400-600ms.

sections.title: Contextual AI: The Missing Piece
sections.summary: Stephenson identifies the critical gap: current pipeline components don't pass context to each other, causing 10-20% of turns to misfire. He proposes 'contextual AI' where each stage accepts context (text, audio, images, embeddings, prior turns) and outputs context, enabling emotion awareness, pace detection, tone instructions from text-to-text to TTS, and feedback from TTS. He predicts this will be how systems are built within the next year, making agents feel genuinely human.

sections.title: Controllability, COGS, and Platform Vision
sections.summary: Stephenson addresses multimodal/speech-to-speech models: merging everything reduces controllability, which enterprises like banks need. He advocates compartmentalized architectures where compute can be concentrated where precision matters most. He discusses COGS optimization through right-sizing each component and positions Deepgram as the platform for low-latency audio AI, noting their TTS is already better than Amazon's.

sections.title: Voice AI Agent Product Announcement
sections.summary: Stephenson briefly notes Deepgram's neural TTS models are not quite as good as 11 Labs, then announces Deepgram's full-stack voice AI agent product, available in preview. Customers can bring their own API keys and LLMs or use Deepgram end-to-end; the integrated approach reduces turn-taking latency to 300-600ms versus 800-1500ms when self-assembled. He shares a QR code and link for access, mentions a workshop by Damen two days prior, and offers $250 in trial credits for anyone to try it out.
